documents.unit: Office of the Provost and Division of Student Affairs
documents.title: Academic Integrity Policy Reminder (letter to students)
documents.summary: A 2023 letter from the Provost and the Dean of Students reminding students that CMU's academic integrity policy bars unauthorized assistance, which includes generative AI unless the instructor permits it. It sends students to their syllabi, their instructors and Computing Services guidance.
documents.stance_why: The letter says the Academic Integrity Policy "prohibits 'unauthorized assistance,' which would include generative AI tools unless explicitly permitted by the instructor." AI is banned unless an instructor permits it, so the document is restrict, although it also hands specifics to syllabi.

units.why: The letter reminds students that the academic integrity policy bars "unauthorized assistance," which "would include generative AI tools unless explicitly permitted by the instructor." AI is therefore banned unless an instructor permits it, which is the fallback rule (P06) rather than a per-instructor rule (P04, next unit).
units.anchor: which would include generative AI tools unless explicitly permitted by the instructor
units.frag_start: Review CMU's existing Academic Integrity Policy
units.policy: CMU's Academic Integrity Policy prohibits unauthorized assistance, which includes generative AI tools unless the instructor explicitly permits them.

units.why: Students are told to "carefully review your course syllabi to understand what is and is not acceptable in each of your courses." The rule is set course by course, which is P04; P11 (no carry-over) is only implied, so P04 fits better.
units.anchor: Carefully review your course syllabi to understand what is and is not acceptable
units.frag_end: generative AI tools in your coursework
units.policy: Students carefully review each course syllabus to understand what is and is not acceptable in each course in terms of using generative AI tools in coursework.

units.why: The letter says "Talk to your instructors if you have questions about these policies or syllabi," which tells students who are unsure to ask the instructor, matching P10.
units.anchor: Talk to your instructors if you have questions about these policies or syllabi
units.frag_start: Talk to your instructors if you
units.frag_end: adhering to our highest academic standards

units.why: The letter directs students to Computing Services generative AI guidelines and "Guidelines for Data Classification" for best practices. This points to vetted guidance on data handling, so P50 fits; it is a referral, not a ban, hence neutral.
units.anchor: Refer to Computing Services' Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines and Guidelines for Data Classification
units.policy: Students refer to Computing Services' Generative Artificial Intelligence Guidelines and Guidelines for Data Classification to learn about generative AI best practices.

units.why: The letter states the goal of addressing challenges and leaning "into the opportunities" of generative AI "by ensuring you have clear guidance and expectations." It is a university-level statement of purpose, so P56 (framework or preamble) fits.
units.anchor: address their challenges and lean into the opportunities they make possible
units.frag_start: As we all continue to learn
units.frag_end: clear guidance and expectations about this technology

documents.unit: Eberly Center for Teaching Excellence and Educational Innovation
documents.title: Examples of possible academic integrity policies that address student use of generative AI tools
tiers: Students may NOT use generative AI in any form (Examples 1-2)
Students are fully encouraged to use generative AI, with citation (Examples 3-4)
Students may use generative AI in some cases but not others (Examples 5-6)
documents.summary: The Eberly Center offers six sample syllabus statements for instructors to adapt, from a full ban to full encouragement with citation. The samples are advisory, and each treats violations as academic integrity violations.
documents.stance_why: The page says the examples "represent a range of options one could adapt or adopt," and sets no single rule. It lists samples that range from "may NOT use generative AI in any form" to "fully encouraged" and "some cases, but not others," so the stance is delegates with tiers.

units.why: The page frames the examples as "a range of options one could adapt or adopt," so the university center leaves the choice to each instructor, which is P04; it is informative, not binding.
units.anchor: a range of options one could adapt or adopt
units.frag_start: The following examples represent a range
units.policy: The sample statements are a range of options instructors can adapt or adopt based on their teaching context and course learning objectives.

units.why: Example 1 says "you should complete all graded assignments in this course yourself, without any use of generative artificial intelligence." That is a default ban on graded work in the sample course, P01.
units.anchor: complete all graded assignments in this course yourself, without any use of generative artificial intelligence
units.frag_start: you should complete all graded assignments

units.why: "To best support your own learning" gives the reason for the Example 1 ban: doing the work yourself builds learning. It is a rationale, P41.
units.anchor: To best support your own learning
units.frag_start: To best support your own learning
units.frag_end: without any use of generative artificial intelligence (AI)
units.policy: Completing graded assignments yourself, without generative AI, best supports your own learning.

units.why: Students are asked to "refrain from using AI tools to generate any content (text, video, audio, images, code, etc.)." This forbids AI producing submitted work, P19, not just a general ban.
units.anchor: refrain from using AI tools to generate any content
units.frag_end: for an assignment or classroom exercise
units.policy: Students refrain from using AI tools to generate any content (text, video, audio, images, code, etc.) for an assignment or classroom exercise.

units.why: "Passing off any AI generated content as your own ... constitutes a violation of CMU's academic integrity policy" classifies the act as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: constitutes a violation of CMU's academic integrity policy
units.frag_start: Passing off any AI generated content
units.policy: Passing off any AI generated content as your own (e.g., cutting and pasting content into written assignments, or paraphrasing AI content) constitutes a violation of CMU's academic integrity policy.

units.why: "If you have any questions about using generative AI in this course please email or talk to me" tells unsure students to ask the instructor, P10.
units.anchor: If you have any questions about using generative AI in this course please email or

units.why: "I expect that all work students submit for this course will be their own" requires submitted work to be the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: I expect that all work students submit for this course will be their own

units.why: "Doing your own work, without human or artificial intelligence assistance, is best for your achievement of the learning objectives" explains the ban by learning, P41.
units.anchor: Doing your own work, without human or artificial intelligence assistance, is best for your achievement
units.frag_start: Doing your own work, without human
units.policy: Doing your own work, without human or artificial intelligence assistance, is best for achievement of the course learning objectives.

units.why: "I specifically forbid the use of ChatGPT or any other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools at all stages of the work process, including brainstorming" is a blanket default ban, even on brainstorming, so P01 not P15.
units.anchor: I specifically forbid the use of ChatGPT or any other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: "Deviations from these guidelines will be considered violations of CMU's academic integrity policy" makes unauthorized AI use misconduct, P36. It recurs in Example 3, which I do not code again.
units.anchor: Deviations from these guidelines will be considered violations of
units.policy: Deviations from these guidelines are considered violations of CMU's academic integrity policy.

units.why: "Expectations for plagiarism, cheating, and acceptable assistance on student work may vary across your courses and instructors" says rules are course-specific, P11. It repeats in Examples 3 and 5 and is not coded again.
units.anchor: expectations for “plagiarism, cheating, and acceptable assistance” on student work may vary across your courses
units.policy: Expectations for plagiarism, cheating, and acceptable assistance on student work may vary across courses and instructors.

units.why: "Please ask me if you have questions regarding what is permissible and not for a particular course or assignment" invites questions before use, P10.
units.anchor: Please ask me if you have questions regarding what is permissible

units.why: Example 3 says "I encourage students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools ... for all assignments and assessments," a default of encouraging AI, P02.
units.anchor: I encourage students to explore the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools

units.why: "Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" requires disclosure with the submission, P24.
units.anchor: Any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited
units.frag_end: guidelines established by the APA Style Guide
units.policy: Any use of generative AI must be appropriately acknowledged and cited, following the guidelines established by the APA Style Guide.

units.why: The citation must include "the specific version of the tool used," a detail requirement on the citation, P25.
units.anchor: including the specific version of the tool used
units.frag_end: specific version of the tool used
units.policy: The citation of generative AI use includes the specific version of the tool used.

units.why: "Submitted work should include the exact prompt ... as well as the AI's full response in an Appendix" requires submitting the record of the AI exchange. I chose P26 over P25 because the whole prompt and response are submitted, not just cited.
units.anchor: Submitted work should include the exact prompt used to generate the content
units.policy: Submitted work includes the exact prompt used to generate the content as well as the AI's full response in an Appendix.

units.why: "It is each student's responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any generative AI output" says AI output may be inaccurate and must be checked, P31.
units.anchor: it is each student's responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any generative AI
units.policy: Because AI generated content is not necessarily accurate or appropriate, it is each student's responsibility to assess the validity and applicability of any generative AI output that is submitted.

units.why: "You may not earn full credit if inaccurate, invalid, or inappropriate information is found in your work" states a grade consequence in advance, P37.
units.anchor: You may not earn full credit if inaccurate, invalid, or inappropriate information is found in

units.why: "You are welcome to use generative AI programs (ChatGPT, DALL-E, etc.) in this course" welcomes AI by default, P02.
units.anchor: You are welcome to use generative AI programs (ChatGPT, DALL-E, etc.) in this course

units.why: The passage calls AI "a personalized learning tool" that can help "generate new ideas." I chose P12 (tutor for learning) over P15 because the passage frames AI as a learning aid, not a technique for one task.
units.anchor: or serving as a personalized learning tool
units.policy: Generative AI programs can be powerful tools for learning and other productive pursuits, including completing some assignments in less time, helping generate new ideas, or serving as a personalized learning tool.

units.why: The policy applies to uncited use "whether that work is created by human beings alone or in collaboration with a generative AI." This treats AI like any other source under existing rules, P45.
units.anchor: whether that work is created by human beings alone or in collaboration with a generative
units.policy: CMU's academic integrity policy applies to all uncited or improperly cited use of content, whether created by human beings alone or in collaboration with a generative AI.

units.why: "you are required to cite the tool's contribution to your work" requires disclosure of AI use, P24.
units.anchor: you are required to cite the tool's contribution to your work
units.frag_start: If you use a generative AI

units.why: "using any generative AI tool without appropriate acknowledgement will be treated as plagiarism" makes nondisclosure itself the violation, P28 (rather than P36, which covers misuse generally).
units.anchor: using any generative AI tool without appropriate acknowledgement will be treated as plagiarism

units.why: "You can include AI generated content verbatim into a writing assignment with quotations and a citation" permits AI text under conditions, P18 (prose).
units.anchor: You can include AI generated content verbatim into a writing assignment with quotations and a

units.why: "You can paraphrase AI generated content with a citation" permits paraphrase of AI prose if cited, P18.
units.anchor: You can paraphrase AI generated content with a citation

units.why: AI-generated "images, video, code, etc." may be included "with an appropriate citation, when expressly permitted in the assignment prompt," so AI code is allowed under stated conditions, P16.
units.anchor: You can include non-text AI generated content (images, video, code, etc.) with an appropriate citation

units.why: "You will conduct your own research and generate bibliographies yourself" requires students to do the research themselves instead of having AI produce it, P19.
units.anchor: You will conduct your own research and generate bibliographies yourself

units.why: "You will not use or present generative AI content that you pass off as your own work" forbids passing off AI output as own, P19.
units.anchor: You will not use or present generative AI content that you pass off as your

units.why: The passage warns that tools "frequently provide users with incorrect information, create professional-looking citations that are not real," which is a warning that output is often wrong, P31.
units.anchor: generative AI tools frequently provide users with incorrect information, create professional-looking citations that are not
units.policy: Generative AI tools frequently provide users with incorrect information, create professional-looking citations that are not real, and generate contradictory statements.

units.why: "incorporate copyrighted material without appropriate attribution" names a copyright risk of AI output, P52.
units.anchor: incorporate copyrighted material without appropriate attribution
units.policy: Generative AI tools sometimes incorporate copyrighted material without appropriate attribution.

units.why: "sometimes integrate biased or offensive concepts" names bias as a harm of AI, P53.
units.anchor: sometimes integrate biased or offensive concepts
units.policy: Generative AI tools sometimes integrate biased or offensive concepts.

units.why: "Code generation models may produce inaccurate outputs" warns that AI code can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: Code generation models may produce inaccurate outputs

units.why: "you understand you are ultimately responsible for the content that you submit" makes the student answerable for all submitted work, P29.
units.anchor: you are ultimately responsible for the content that you submit

units.why: "Work that is inaccurate, biased, unethical, offensive, plagiarized, or incorrect will be treated as such during the evaluation of your work" says evaluation penalizes flawed AI-derived work, P37.
units.anchor: Work that is inaccurate, biased, unethical, offensive, plagiarized, or incorrect will be treated as such

units.why: "Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of generative artificial intelligence" makes the rule vary by assignment, P04.
units.anchor: Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of generative artificial

units.why: "When AI use is permissible, it will be clearly stated in the assignment prompt posted in Canvas" commits the instructor to state expectations in assignment instructions, P09.
units.anchor: it will be clearly stated in the assignment prompt posted in Canvas

units.why: "Otherwise, the default is that use of generative AI is disallowed" states what applies when an assignment is silent, P06.
units.anchor: Otherwise, the default is that use of generative AI is disallowed

units.why: "In assignments where generative AI tools are allowed, their use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" requires disclosure, P24.
units.anchor: their use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited

units.why: The sample note "I generated this work through Chat GPT and edited the content for accuracy" shows the form of a disclosure statement for a fully generated document, P24.
units.anchor: I generated this work through Chat GPT and edited the content for accuracy
units.policy: If the whole document is generated through ChatGPT and edited for accuracy, the submitted work includes a note such as: I generated this work through Chat GPT and edited the content for accuracy.

units.why: "Paraphrasing or quoting smaller samples of AI generated content must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" is a disclosure rule for partial use, P24.
units.anchor: Paraphrasing or quoting smaller samples of AI generated content must be appropriately acknowledged and cited

units.why: "Deviations from the guidelines above will be considered violations of CMU's academic integrity policy" makes departures misconduct, P36. Wording differs from Example 2, so I code it.
units.anchor: Deviations from the guidelines above will be considered violations of

units.why: "use of generative AI will be limited to exercises during class sessions" allows AI only in class exercises. The rule is set per activity, so P04 rather than P02.
units.anchor: use of generative AI will be limited to exercises during class sessions

units.why: "I will always indicate when and where use of AI tools during class sessions is appropriate (and not)" commits the instructor to state expectations for each activity, P09.
units.anchor: I will always indicate when and where use of AI tools during class sessions is

units.why: "Learning how to use AI is an emerging skill" and the plan to "better understand their benefits and limitations" mean the course teaches AI use in class, P44.
units.anchor: Learning how to use AI is an emerging skill
units.policy: During some class sessions, the instructor may leverage generative AI tools to support learning, to let students explore how they can be used, and to better understand their benefits and limitations; learning how to use AI is an emerging skill.

units.why: Examples of in-class use include "brainstorming new ideas," so brainstorming with AI is permitted in ungraded class exercises, P15.
units.anchor: brainstorming new ideas
units.frag_end: different ways to talk about a problem
units.policy: Examples of use during ungraded classroom exercises include brainstorming new ideas, developing example outlines or approaches to your work, and generating different ways to talk about a problem.

units.why: "you may not use AI tools to generate work for an assignment to be submitted for a grade" forbids AI producing graded work, P19.
units.anchor: may not use AI tools to generate work for an assignment to be submitted for
units.frag_end: represented by the learning objectives of this course
units.policy: You may not use AI tools to generate work for an assignment to be submitted for a grade.

units.why: "this cannot be considered a substitute for developing the fundamental skills and expertise" explains the ban by skill-building, P41.
units.anchor: cannot be considered a substitute for developing the fundamental skills and expertise
units.policy: AI-generated work for a graded assignment cannot be considered a substitute for developing the fundamental skills and expertise represented by the learning objectives of this course.

units.why: AI tools "rely on predictive models to generate content that may appear correct, but has been shown to sometimes be incomplete, inaccurate" is a caution that output can be wrong, P31.
units.anchor: content that may appear correct, but has been shown to sometimes be incomplete, inaccurate
units.policy: Generative AI tools rely on predictive models to generate content that may appear correct but has sometimes been incomplete, inaccurate, taken without attribution from other sources, and/or biased.

units.why: "an AI tool should not be considered a substitute for traditional approaches to research" says AI must not replace the student's own research and thinking, P32.
units.anchor: an AI tool should not be considered a substitute for traditional approaches to research

units.why: "you should complete all graded assignments without any assistance from AI tools" is a default ban on graded work in this sample, P01.
units.anchor: you should complete all graded assignments without any assistance from AI tools

units.why: "You are ultimately responsible for the content of the information you submit and may not attempt to pass off any work generated by an AI program as your own" holds the student responsible, P29.
units.anchor: You are ultimately responsible for the content of the information you submit

notes: Coder A. Provost letter is thin (2023). Eberly page is advisory sample text; units are coded as the sample policies state them. Repeated sentences across examples (Deviations..., Note that expectations...) were coded once, except where the wording differs. The Example 5 sentence 'You may not earn full credit' was skipped because the saved text splits the word 'You'; Example 3 covers the same rule.
